records.title: Editorial: Underlying neurobiological, genetic, and behavioral mechanisms in schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder
records.abstract: Understanding potential joint underlying mechanisms of Schizophrenia (SZ) and Autism Spectrum Disorder (AT) is an essential area of study given their phenotypic overlap, including in social communication and social cognition differences1. This research topic sought to invite contributions from researchers to share new scientific evidence on the common and distinct phenotypes and underlying mechanisms between and within SZand AT by employing diverse clinical, behavioral, and neuroscience techniques (e.g., neuroimaging, electrophysiology, genetics, symptom characterization, neurocognitive assessments). The overarching goal of this topic of research is to shed light on the functional significance of symptom profiles and find routes to common new venues for interventions in AT and SZ. The studies shown in this research topic reflect the growth of the current scientific landscape, illustrating the broadening of the standard techniques to new territories and their aim to discover possible common mechanistic pathways. While research directly comparing AT and SZ is not common, few contributions to this topic compared their clinical and cognitive profiles. Nakamura et al. 2 aimed to identify clinical similarities and differences in AT and SZ and proposed a new useful objective predictive model that could aid with differential diagnosis. For that purpose, the authors used a combination of items from assessments validated and typically used in one of the groups only, including the Autism Diagnostic observation Schedule, 2nd edition (ADOS-2) and the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) to develop a predictive diagnostic model. Their studies revealed that negative symptoms in SZ elevated the ADOS-2 ratings and the ADOS-2 false-positive rates of SZ. Therefore, their proposed predictive model to distinguish SZ and AT included a combination of specific ADOS-2 items (A7, A10, B1, B6, B8, and B9). The study of Nakamura et al., 2 echoed the findings from previous studies by Trevisan et al. 3 and Corbera et al. 4, highlighting the need for better, cross-diagnostic symptom measures for differential diagnosis, given the heterogeneity in clinical presentation of both disorders. Other studies have attempted to examine the shared dysfunctions in these disorders by focusing on neurocognitive profiles instead of symptom profiles. For example, Morais et al.5 examined the executive functioning (EF) profiles in AT, SZ and neurotypical (NT) individuals. Their outcomes showed a substantial overlap in EF deficits with only a few differences in working memory; thus, they suggested tailoring cognitive remediation interventions to these deficits in both populations. While the sample size in this study is relatively small (n=15/group), and results should be replicated, it supports similar interventions for both AT and SZ5. Complementing this, in their review, Guerrera et al.6 advocated for a neurodevelopmental perspective when examining SZ and AT, encouraging the development of large longitudinal studies comparing their phenotypic profile from childhood. Individual studies into disorder-specific mechanisms can also provide valuable insights. For example, the study by Chen et al.7 investigated social-emotional interference in AT children with IQ>80 using an experimental design with modified flanker tasks. Their study provided insightful information about emotional processing in autistic children as they showed that they struggle more than typically developing controls in controlling interference from social information, and that they faced more difficulties as the information load increased, which could hinder their ability to adapt to and engage in social situations. The authors proposed practical, translational strategies offering direct implications for intervention in complex social scenarios such as providing a gradual exposure transition from virtual faces to real faces, and from single faces to different faces. Even though this study focused solely on AT, it provided a potential early biomarker to target for future studies potentially applicable to SZ, and warranting future cross-disorder research. While genetic studies examining the risk of autism have grown over the years, fewer have examined the interaction between genetic and environmental risk factors. The study by Zhang et al.8 focused on examining telomere length (TL), considered to be a biomarker of cumulative intracellular oxidative stress (OS) in autism. This study showed a relationship between TL shortening and oxidative damage in AT and underscores the potential value of measuring OS-related biomarkers in autism for early diagnosis and interventions. Therefore, comparing the role of OS imbalance in the pathophysiology of AT and SZ is an additional area of further research and a promising area for the generation of treatment interventions. Studying genomic information involves the use of large-scale, well-powered studies. In this regard, Mas et al.9 proposed the development of a large-scale multicenter study involved in the development and validation of predictive algorithms to classify first-episode psychosis (FEP) patients according to their response to antipsychotics, to select the most appropriate treatment strategy for each patient. In this large protocol, Mas et al. 9 propose to employ machine learning techniques to integrate predictors, such as pharmacogenetic, epigenetic, and clinical data, and sociodemographic, environmental, and neuroanatomical data, to enhance personalized medicine. This proposed protocol highlights the importance of the interplay of pharmacogenomic studies and precision medicine as a translational step to applicability to clinical practice, an area without doubt, of scarcity in the comparison of SZ and AT. Among the innovative contributions to this topic, the study by Li et al.10 performed a systematic search of 30 clinical studies aimed to examine the gut microbiota in patients with SZ, as previous reports had shown changes in the composition of the gut microbiota in mental conditions. They10 reported a consistent dysbiosis of microbiota in SZ and a large heterogeneity of SZ in these measurements. There is a paucity of research in this area, especially in comparative studies examining the gut-brain axis and the role of alterations in the gut microbiota in the pathogenesis of SZ and AT, which we encourage future researchers to pursue. Finally, Ni et al. (2024)11 aimed at examining the causal link between chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) risk and SZ using trans-ethnic Mendelian randomization analyses, employing data from public genome-wide association studies (GWAS) datasets. The authors found a causal relationship but mediated by variables such as body mass index (BMI), smoking, and major depressive disorder, only in individuals with European ancestry. Additionally, Ni et al.11 raised a concern about the scarcity of studies on this topic in autism. Given the conflicting evidence in the prevalence of asthma in this population, and the common vulnerabilities between SZ and AT, this is another area where further research can explore mediators of the link to COPD, in larger scale GWAS studies, and with diverse ancestral populations. Looking ahead, future research should continue to prioritize transdiagnostic approaches that examine shared and distinct mechanisms across SZ and AT, with a focus on integrative models that combine genetic, environmental, neurobiological, and behavioral data. Large-scale, longitudinal studies are essential to disentangle developmental trajectories and identify early biomarkers that could aid in both prediction and intervention. Moreover, machine learning and precision medicine approaches should be increasingly applied not only to pharmacogenomic studies but also to refine diagnostic classification, considering potential subtypes across the SZ-AT spectrum, and personalize intervention strategies. Finally, future research should explore how to integrate digital phenotyping, real-time behavioral monitoring, and neurotechnological innovations that could provide dynamic, individualized insights into symptom trajectories and intervention outcome. Developing standardized, cross-disorder assessment tools and scalable interventions grounded in shared cognitive, genetic or neural differences holds promise for improving diagnostic precision and outcomes.

records.title: Influence of leader humility on subordinates’ knowledge-sharing: exploring the boundary conditions
records.abstract:
Among the human aspects of leaders, humility has gained traction in recent explorations. Subordinates’ psychological safety has been established to mediate between leader humility and subordinates’ knowledge sharing. However, because knowledge sharing is a complicated phenomenon driven by situational demands and individual characteristics, the authors project the presence of boundary conditions in the influence of leader humility on knowledge sharing through psychological safety. The purpose of this study is to investigate the moderating effect of leader competence on the relationship between leader humility and psychological safety, as well as the moderating effect of subordinates’ occupational self-efficacy (OSE) on the relationship between psychological safety and subordinates’ knowledge sharing, within the framework of the social information processing (SIP) theory.
 
 
 
 The authors used a time-lagged, three-wave survey-based questionnaire. Responses from 392 employees working in the Indian IT organizations, collected by using judgmental sampling techniques, were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling.
 
 
 
 Results confirm that leader humility influences subordinates’ knowledge sharing through psychological safety. Findings also prove moderation by leader competence between leader humility and psychological safety and by OSE between psychological safety and subordinates’ knowledge sharing.
 
 
 
 The authors have considered leader humility as a human aspect of a leader and examined the boundary conditions of knowledge sharing through leader humility. Results demonstrate that psychological safety promotes knowledge sharing as a mediator and is strengthened by leader competence and subordinates’ OSE as relatively under-explored moderators. This study illustrates how leader humility and competence jointly influence subordinates’ knowledge sharing via psychological safety. The authors have also positioned OSE as a moderator within the SIP framework and substantiated that knowledge sharing is influenced by subordinates’ cognitive and motivational inclination, besides leader competence.

records.title: Item-based Parsing of Dynamic Scenes in a Combined Attentional Tracking and Working Memory Task.
records.abstract: Human visual processing is limited-we can only track a few moving objects at a time and store a few items in visual working memory (WM). A shared mechanism that may underlie these performance limits is how the visual system parses a scene into representational units. In the present study, we explored whether multiple-object tracking (MOT) and WM rely on a common item-based indexing mechanism. We measured the contralateral delay activity (CDA), an event-related slow wave that tracks load in an item-based manner, as participants completed a combined WM and MOT task, concurrently tracking items and remembering visual information. In Experiment 1, participants tracked one or two moving discs without needing to remember the discs' colors (track and ignore condition) or while also remembering the discs' colors (two or four colors in total; track and remember condition). In Experiment 2, participants attended either two static discs or two moving discs, while remembering the discs' colors (two or four colors). In both experiments, the CDA was largely determined by the tracking task-CDA amplitudes reflected the number of tracked discs and not the number of to-be-remembered colors. However, when the discs were static, the CDA amplitudes did reflect color load. We discuss this set of findings in relation to longstanding theories of visual cognition (fingers of instantiation and object files) and the implications for cognitive models of representation of visual information-that how a scene is parsed into item-based representations is a key mechanism in the operation of WM.

records.title: Public Opinion and Expert Critique: Reconsidering the Role of Constitutional Scholars in Japan’s Security Policy
records.abstract: Do experts’ opinions influence public opinion? Although experts with academic backgrounds are gaining a presence in policy debates, empirical studies deliver inconclusive results on whether experts have a cueing effect. Moreover, while most studies focus on cases where experts propose or recommend policies, the influence of their criticism on government policy has not received much research attention. To fill this gap, through an online survey in Japan, we test the effect of constitutional scholars’ criticism on people’s support for a dispatch of the Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF). Since constitutional academics, regarded as influential experts, have historically criticized the constitutional legitimacy of Japan’s security policy, they provide a suitable case to examine. The results show that such criticism has no causal effect on public attitudes even among the most liberal respondents or those with high confidence in constitutional scholars. Contrary opinions from retired general officers decreased support for the dispatch among individuals who were conservative or had high confidence in the JSDF. These findings imply that though people consciously sift through information from different sources, they mostly reject the opinions of academic experts.

records.title: THE EFFECTS OF LEARNER EXPERTISE ON INTRINSIC, EXTRANEOUS AND GERMANE COGNITIVE LOAD THROUGH INSTRUCTIONAL VIDEOS: AN EXPLORATORY ANALYSIS
“Lavender Haze” in the Airways
records.abstract:
Introduction
Taylor Swift has dominated global press in recent years through the success of her Eras Tour, her use of authenticity in branding (Khanal 234), and her choreographed engagement with fans (Bengtsson and Edlom 65). Swift has also faced criticism regarding carbon emissions, for her use of a private jet in service of her career (Olmstead 652; Hammons 154). Said criticism is often made through the lens of anti-fandom, detraction based on hate for or trivialisation of a celebrity or media property (Duffy et al. 8). While this arguably follows a long tradition of activists using the issue-attention cycle (Downs) to bring awareness to a cause, awareness alone as a tactic has been shown to be ineffective in sustaining social change, including with ecoactivism specifically (McDonald 54-55). Further, anti-fandom activism relies on outgroup hate, which has been shown to be less effective than the tactics of in-group love (Nettasinghe et al. 567) used by fan activists. While Swift’s carbon footprint is large (Haneman 210) and private jets are a broader systemic problem in the battle to reduce global carbon emissions (Olmstead 667), to critique Swift’s emissions as an individual also misses how she is functionally an enterprise (Zheng 1874) within an industry that has a broader impact on climate change (Hammons 174; Thomson et al. 13). Anti-fan criticism of Swift ignores her status as a brand, often generating media attention rather than holding Swift and other celebrities accountable or driving other direct action towards curtailing climate change. This article seeks to explore anti-fan action against Taylor Swift as a tactic of ecoactivism and ecopolitics, as well as arguing for a more nuanced approach which seeks to mobilise an already active pro-Swift fandom towards more sustainable, effective collective action.
Contextualising Taylor Swift
Critiques of Swift’s jet use have often compared her to the average individual, non-celebrity, emitter (Haneman 210) or lampooned said use as though she is simply running coffee errands (Hammons 154). Swift as a public figure, however, is more an enterprise than an individual. While the exact number of people employed by Swift is not publicly known, the singer/songwriter operates as the umbrella enterprise for multiple companies including 13 Management (her core management team) and Taylor Swift Tours (band, backup singers and dancers, drivers, and other crew). Swift additionally employs a marketing and public relations firm as well as regularly holding contracts for merchandising, music production, hair, makeup, and more. While Swift’s jet emissions in 2022 were estimated to have a social cost of over $400,000 (Haneman 210), her Eras Tour the following two years was responsible for restoring some economic markets to pre-pandemic levels or higher (Hoff et al.; Sidebottom 2), adding $4.3 billion to the United States gross domestic product alone (Burman). The economic effect on cities that hosted the Eras Tour was so consistent and prolific that it garnered the name “Swiftonomics” (Khanal 234).
Meanwhile, the tour itself became the highest grossing music tour of all time, netting $2,077,618,725 in ticket sales and roughly $400 million in merchandise sales (Savage). For comparison, Swift’s ticket sales from 17 March 2023 to 8 December 2024 were roughly equivalent to Boeing’s record-setting 2021 fiscal e-commerce sales (Boeing). This is not to say that her earnings or economic contributions bar her from criticism, but rather that anti-fan eco-based criticisms draw on false equivalencies. If Swift is to be a target of ecoactivism, she should be targeted as a multinational enterprise and prioritised as a target based on her emissions in comparison to other industrial carbon emitters, with the same considerations given to social cost vs. social gain analyses.
Touring, however, is not the only business Swift engages in. She of course writes, records, and sells music, but she also engages in the business of sustaining her fandom through the deliberate cultivation of a parasocial relationship with her fans. Swift accomplishes this through a very specific type of branding and marketing which relies on a narrative of authenticity (Khanal 234) and choreographed engagement with fans (Bengtsson and Edlom 65). Whether it is her expression of her values or the demeanor with which she carries herself during public controversies (Karulkar et al. 1), the fannish aura surrounding Swift is one of shared knowing. It is a parasocial relationship in which fans are meant to feel akin to friends of Swift and thus feel inclined to support Swift beyond her music. 
While a parasocial relationship is inherently lopsided (no one outside of Swift’s inner circle is really able to know her), Swift’s utilisation of her fans’ support is more interactive than many other parasocial relationships. Fans, for example, experience some sense of actually knowing Swift through the personal vulnerabilities she chooses to share in her song lyrics, and fans see said lyrics as authentic (Khanal 231). Likewise, Swift has been said to have cultivated a sense of “nostalgic girlhood” which evokes a sense of shared space, one which mimics slumber parties and shared bedrooms (Morris 90-91). Swift also sometimes interacts directly with fans on a more personal level, attending weddings, sending gifts, and covering tuition payments (Khanal 234). She even once invited fans to a dance party in her home wherein she served them homemade cookies (Khanal 234).
Since her brand is based around authenticity, any meaningful public critique of Swift, ecoactivist or otherwise, would need to effectively attack her authenticity. This tactic was very nearly successful during a public feud with Kanye West and Kim Kardashian in 2016 which attempted to paint Swift as a liar and a snake over an edited conversation between the three about how Swift was portrayed in one of West’s songs. However, through fan engagement with transmedia campaigns, Swift was ultimately able to regain control of the public narrative about herself (Zafina and Sinha 12). She even used the imagery of the snake, and her jet, to satirise her critics (“Look What You Made Me Do”). This was before ecoactivist criticism, when the jet was being used by anti-fans as a symbol of Swift’s wealth (Lang), in an effort to delegitimise her authenticity and imply she was greedy and out of touch with her fan-base.
Following the 2016 feud and eventual comeback, fans who remained loyal throughout, as well as those who eventually sided with Swift’s version of events, became protective of Swift’s reputation moving forward (Zafina and Sinha 12). This loyalty was then later extended to another public feud she had with Big Machine Records, specifically with investor and record executive Scooter Braun, over the sale of the master recordings of her first six studio albums. After attempting to purchase the masters herself, unsuccessfully, Swift chose to take a bold gamble by re-recording four of the six albums in an effort to regain the rights to her own, original work. Fans were so supportive of Swift’s rereleasing her own music, through streaming and album sales, that Swift changed the industry standard for musician ownership and reclamation of sold work, especially for young, women artists (Neal 84-85). To subvert brand loyalty, anti-fan ecoactivism targeting Swift would thus only be effective if it could rebrand Swift as betraying the public and her fans, and she never promised lower carbon emissions to either.
Carbon Emissions 
Between January and August 2022, Swift’s private plane was at the top of the charts, so to speak, for its carbon footprint, totaling 170 flights and 8,293 tons of emissions (Godlewski 3). However, Swift’s plane has not stayed in even the top 15 celebrity jets responsible for the most carbon emissions as of 2024 (Ring). This is not necessarily due to increased responsibility on Swift’s part, though it should be noted that, like other businesses, Swift’s public relations team has shared that she purchases carbon offsets as part of her air travel and purchases more than double what is recommended based on her mileage (O’Malley). Carbon offsets, or funding for projects which otherwise reduce emissions, are arguably themselves not a viable long-term tactic in addressing climate change, due to complexities and variabilities in how they are used and reported (de Mello 164-166), but this ultimately points to the fact that emissions by private jets are a broader systemic issue (Godlewski 1-2), and not a Swift-specific one. Even larger companies with reduced overall carbon emissions following public criticism, like Nike, are seeing increases in emissions due to private jet use (Davis), though the entertainment industry is responsible for some of the highest use of private planes (Hammons 174).
The rise in private jet use and associated carbon emissions is also largely a problem of legislative failures to adequately tax and otherwise restrict their use (Godlewski 26). Additionally, use of private planes by the ultra-famous is somewhat necessitated by inadequate safety measures to protect against harassment by paparazzi and stalkers, without which private planes are the safest form of travel, and frequently the most efficient for high-profile individuals (Olmstead 663-665). This is not to say that individual safety trumps the public good of reduced carbon emission, but to say that Swift’s jet use is multifactorial and more complex than simply asking that she use the jet less.
It is also worth noting that, while touring, recording, and promoting within the music industry currently relies heavily on ecologically inefficient private planes for top-billed artists like Swift, private jets are not responsible for the majority of carbon emissions associated with music production, celebrity, and fandom. records.title: <b>METHODS OF SUMMARIZING CHESS TOPICS IN PRIMARY SCHOOL </b>
records.abstract: The mandatory integration of chess into mainstream primary education necessitates the development of effective formative assessment strategies that authentically align with the interactive and dynamic nature of the game. However, traditional summative evaluations often induce cognitive overload and academic anxiety, thereby hindering long-term knowledge retention and student motivation. To address this methodological gap, this mixed-methods study empirically evaluates the efficacy of newly designed, culturally responsive gamified instructional techniques—specifically applied during the summarization phase of chess lessons. Conducted within the Armenian state education system, the quasi-experimental intervention involved 144 primary school students (grades 2–4) who were evenly divided into experimental and control cohorts across a 12-week academic semester. Quantitative analyses revealed that the experimental group achieved notably higher summative outcomes (Cohen’s d = 0.78) and demonstrated improved cognitive retention over the 12-week semester, particularly in spatial reasoning. Concurrently, qualitative observations indicated that within the gamified context, these assessments positively influenced classroom dynamics. The experimental cohort exhibited increased intrinsic motivation and more frequent elaborative peer scaffolding compared to standard instruction, although further research is needed to completely isolate these effects from instructional novelty. The findings indicate that game-based formative assessments effectively mitigate extraneous cognitive load while satisfying the foundational psychological needs of learner autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Ultimately, this research concludes that seamlessly bridging rigorous academic evaluation with interactive gameplay is essential for optimizing cognitive processing and unlocking the comprehensive educational potential of chess for primary school learners.

records.title: Academic Experience Platforms: AI Meets Cognitive Science
records.venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
records.abstract: The growing demand for online and hybrid education has revealed several opportunities for improvement in contemporary educational ecosystems and infrastructure. Traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS) function as content databases with limited personalization capabilities, while corporate Learning Experience Platforms (LXP) emphasize skill acquisition without supporting comprehensive academic activities. The current work proposes the Academic Experience Platform (AXP), an AI-powered system to address knowledge fragmentation, algorithmic transparency, and academic rigor through evidence-based instructional design grounded in established instructional theories. The AXP framework is supported by Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) to address the following critical needs: (1) preventing cognitive overload through intelligent content design which lowers mental overstimulation (extraneous load) while maximizing productive learning efforts (germane load), (2) applying diagnostic assessments that adapt content based on learners' existing knowledge to avoid the expertise reversal effect in which advanced learners waste time on material they've already mastered, and (3) leveraging learning analytics to create personalized pathways while maintaining transparency and learner agency. Unlike existing platforms, the AXP aims to offer pedagogical ecosystems for both instructors and learners. The AXP shall enable instructors in designing evidence-based microlearning modules, implementing diagnostic assessments, and accessing analytics that enhances instructional design. Learners get on-demand access to role-based content, custom organic recommendations, and structured progressions from lower-order to higher-order thinking skills aligned with Bloom's Taxonomy. The framework integrates competency-based education principles with mechanisms to prevent knowledge fragmentation. Learning analytics track concept coverage, identify gaps in knowledge networks, and prompt integration activities, while checkpoint assessments ensure learners progress from isolated skill acquisition to integrated competency. This research contributes theoretical foundations for AXP development and practical design guidelines for educational technology developers, institutional decision-makers, and instructional designers seeking to transform academic delivery models while maintaining rigor and supporting workforce readiness.

records.title: An experimental investigation of the split-attention effect on endoscopic surgical performance.
records.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Surgeons in the operating theatre frequently need to split their attention, such as when switching between the monitor and radiological images during endoscopic surgery. This split attention can lead to cognitive overload, potentially impacting performance. Despite this, limited research has been conducted on how split attention affects surgical outcomes.


PATIENTS AND METHODS
This study examines the impact of split attention on surgical performance in a simulation-based training environment with two conditions: A far-condition (where information sources were spaced farther apart) and a near-condition (where sources were positioned closer together). A total of 53 participants (13 experienced surgical residents and 40 beginners) completed ten trials in each condition.


RESULTS
The results indicated that split attention led to diminished performance in beginners but not in residents. These findings suggest that expertise plays a crucial role in managing cognitive load for surgeons.


CONCLUSION
The study highlights the need to develop training curricula that promote the automation of surgical skills through practice, allowing surgeons to allocate more cognitive resources effectively.

records.title: Appearance–Behavior Framework (ABF) v1.0–v2.5: Complete Visual Compendium of Behavioral Inference, Digital Twins, Network Control, and Closed-Loop Risk Management
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: This release presents the complete visual compendium of the Appearance–Behavior Framework (ABF), covering versions v1.0 through v2.5. ABF is a domain-agnostic inference framework that reconstructs latent behavioral dynamics from observable appearances under uncertainty and constraints. Across five major development stages, the framework progresses from conceptual foundations and mathematical formalization to predictive behavioral science, digital twins, network-level inference, and illustrative closed-loop population-level risk control. The collection contains all 48 figures developed throughout the ABF series: • v1.0–v1.2: Conceptual and mathematical foundations, latent behavior manifolds, Takens embedding, observable signatures, behavioral identifiability, and constraint-based inference. • v1.3: Cross-domain case studies including EEG dynamics (CHB-MIT) and cognitive decline trajectories (ADNI), demonstrating domain generalization. • v1.4: Quantitative appearance–behavior mapping, Bayesian behavioral inference, equifinality theory, identifiability gains, and cross-modal constraint fusion. • v2.0–v2.3: Predictive behavioral science, Behavioral Transformation Risk Score (BTRS), uncertainty propagation, sequential Bayesian digital twins, personalized forecasting, counterfactual intervention simulation, and reinforcement-learning-based adaptive intervention. • v2.4: Multi-Agent Structural Interaction (MASI), Population-BTRS, synthetic network recovery, and network-aware intervention optimization (MAIO). • v2.5: Illustrative closed-loop population-level risk control integrating Lyapunov-inspired stability conditions, Control Barrier Function (CBF) safety shielding, network-aware Model Predictive Control (MPC), adherence feedback updating, multi-agent load balancing, and operational dashboard concepts. This archive includes: - Complete preprint PDF (34 pages)- Full set of Figures 1–48- Demonstration scripts for illustrative figure generation- README documentation All quantitative values, simulations, figures, and control examples are illustrative and conceptual unless explicitly stated otherwise. No real-world clinical validation, causal efficacy claim, policy optimality claim, or deployment claim is made. Zenodo archiving is intended for timestamped scholarly dissemination and version preservation.

records.title: Applying a Scaffolding-Informed Mixed Reality System to Vehicle Engine Disassembly Instruction
Artificial Intelligence Music Platform for Piano Majors Improves Learning and Reduces Anxiety:2Randomized Study with Heart Rate Variability Cues
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied in music pedagogy, yet reproducible workflows that jointly evaluate knowledge acquisition and anxiety regulation remain limited. This protocol describes a randomized controlled workflow for implementing an AI-driven music education platform within routine studio-class teaching and assessing its effects in undergraduate piano majors. Participants are screened and randomly allocated to an AI-driven platform or traditional instruction for 2 weeks (twelve 30-min sessions). Outcomes include a structured music-theory/analysis test and the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory–State (STAI-S; 20 items, 4-point scale; total 20–80). Heart-rate variability (HRV) is recorded during a 5-min seated rest and a 5-min standardized practice segment; primary indices include the root mean square of successive differences of normal-to-normal intervals (RMSSD; short-term vagal activity), the standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN; overall variability), and high-frequency (HF) power (parasympathetic-related spectral component). The protocol enables instructors and researchers to deploy the platform and follow a standardized sequence covering participant screening, randomization execution, platform setup/configuration, HRV sensor placement and recording, artifact handling and HRV computation, administration/scoring of all outcome measures, and final data export, file naming, and secure storage for statistical analysis. Analyses use independent-samples t-tests and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) with baseline as a covariate. Representative results show higher adjusted post-test theory performance in the AI-driven arm (partial η² = 0.206) and lower post-intervention state anxiety ((t(38) = -3.486, p = 0.001; Cohen’s d ≈ 1.10) than controls, with HRV patterns providing physiological context and secondary cognitive-load outcomes indicating reduced extraneous load.

records.title: Beyond total scores: symptom composition as a predictor of recovery according to concussion history
records.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to determine whether early symptom cluster composition at presentation predicts recovery after sport-related concussion, and whether these associations differ by concussion history. METHODS: The authors conducted a retrospective cohort study of athletes aged 12-22 years who were evaluated at their regional concussion center between November 2017 and April 2022. Cluster ratios for cognitive, somatic, and emotional symptoms were calculated as domain sums divided by the initial Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS) score. Primary outcomes were the number of days to return to learn (RTL), symptom resolution (SR), and return to play (RTP). Multivariable linear regression models were fit separately for athletes with no prior concussion and for those with ≥ 1 prior concussion, entering all three cluster ratios and adjusting for age, sex, time to presentation, and a history of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, migraine, and psychiatric conditions. Effect modification was assessed using a hierarchical full-cohort model that included a cognitive ratio × number of prior concussions interaction term. Kaplan-Meier curves were used to assess recovery across strata defined by prior concussion (yes/no) and high versus low cognitive burden (median split), with groups compared using log-rank tests. RESULTS: Of 2086 screened patients, 476 met the inclusion criteria (58.4% with no prior concussion and 41.6% with ≥ 1 prior concussion). Athletes with prior concussion were older (mean age 16.43 ± 1.92 vs 15.67 ± 1.55 years, p < 0.001), more often White (87.8% vs 76.3%, p = 0.011), presented later (mean 3.59 ± 3.34 days vs 2.86 ± 3.13 days, p = 0.016), and had similar initial PCSS scores (mean 29.39 ± 22.07 vs 28.32 ± 22.82, p = 0.607), but longer RTP (mean 33.40 ± 24.46 days vs 27.50 ± 22.34 days, p = 0.017). In multivariable models, symptom cluster ratios were not associated with RTL, SR, or RTP in the no prior concussion group. In the prior concussion group, a higher cognitive cluster ratio was associated with longer RTL (p = 0.020) and independently predicted longer SR (p = 0.003). In whole-cohort models, the interaction between cognitive ratio and prior concussion was significant for SR (p = 0.005), indicating that the adverse impact of cognitive-dominant profiles on recovery increased with the number of prior concussions. Kaplan-Meier analyses showed stepwise delays in RTL, SR, and RTP across cognitive burden-prior concussion strata (SR: log-rank χ2(3) = 10.62, p = 0.014; RTP: χ2(3) = 10.48, p = 0.015; RTL: χ2(3) = 8.10, p = 0.044), with the slowest recovery demonstrated in the group with prior concussion and high cognitive burden. CONCLUSIONS: Symptom composition at presentation is prognostic primarily in athletes with prior concussion. Cognitive-dominant profiles predicted slower SR and RTL in this subgroup, and the adverse effect of cognitive burden on recovery increased with increasing concussion history.

records.title: Boundary conditions of collaborative learning using worked-examples: joint moderating effects of task-specific prior knowledge and task complexity on transfer performance and cognitive load
records.abstract: When collaborative learning facilitates learning, remains a central question in educational research. Grounded in cognitive load theory, this study examined whether the effectiveness of collaborative, relative to individual, learning from worked-examples is jointly moderated by learners’ experimentally induced task-specific prior knowledge and task complexity. A 2 (task-specific prior knowledge: low vs. high) × 2 (task complexity: low vs. high) × 2 (learning condition: individual vs. collaborative) mixed design was employed, with task complexity as a within-subjects factor. A total of 134 fifth-grade students participated in the study. They studied mathematical worked-examples of varying complexity, either individually or collaboratively, and then completed near-transfer and far-transfer tests as well as cognitive load ratings. Results showed a significant three-way interaction among task-specific prior knowledge, task complexity, and learning condition for near-transfer, indicating that the effect of learning condition depended jointly on learners’ task-specific prior knowledge and task complexity. Specifically, under high task complexity, collaborative learning outperformed individual learning among learners with high task-specific prior knowledge, whereas no stable collaborative advantage was found for learners with low task-specific prior knowledge. For far-transfer, the main effects of task-specific prior knowledge and task complexity were significant, whereas the main effect of learning condition and all interaction effects did not reach statistical significance. Thus, collaborative learning did not show a stable advantage in far-transfer tasks. The cognitive load results provided supportive evidence for understanding the differences in transfer performance: students in the collaborative learning condition reported lower subjective cognitive load than those in the individual learning condition, and high complexity tasks elicited higher cognitive load than low complexity tasks. Overall, the findings suggest that the effectiveness of collaboration in learning from worked-examples is conditional rather than universal. Its benefits depend on the fit between task complexity and learners’ task-specific prior knowledge. The study provides empirical evidence on the boundary conditions of collaborative learning in elementary mathematics instruction through worked examples and contributes to a better understanding of when collaborative learning is most effective.

records.title: Brainprint Measurement Under Complex Cognitive Load Scenarios With a Spatially Aware Polyspectral Retention Network
records.venue: IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement
records.abstract: The brainprint, based on electroencephalography (EEG), offers unique identification through dynamic physiological patterns. However, EEGs may concurrently capture cognitive load as a potential interference to brainprint. On the contrary, traditional EEG-based deep models, designed for diagnostic purposes, often treat brainprint variations as noise. To address this mismatch, we introduce the brainprint database under complex cognitive load scenarios (BOOLS) and a novel spatially aware polyspectral retention network (SAPR-Net). The BOOLS database records EEG signals under four different cognitive load levels from 30 participants, which is made publicly available. The SAPR-Net amplifies individual-specific EEG features by improving the connectivity within and between cortical regions, utilizing a new electrode-position encoding method. The peak performance of the SAPR-Net on the BOOLS database was achieved at 94.70%. Through analysis of channel selection strategies and window size choices, we demonstrate that the brainprint can be consistently preserved despite cognitive load fluctuations by leveraging interpretable EEG connectivity.

records.title: Can explainable AI scaffolding reduce cognitive load and enhance embodied expression? A quasi-experimental study of multilingual vocal learning in Bel Canto education
records.abstract: Exploring how artificial intelligence technology can effectively support music education has become a critical issue in the digital era. This study addresses the high cognitive load and embodied expression difficulties faced by bel canto students when learning multilingual vocal works, designing and validating the educational effectiveness of an explainable AI scaffolding learning system. The study employed a 2 × 3 mixed-factor quasi-experimental design, with 64 college students from the Conservatory of Music allocated to the XAI scaffolding group and the traditional AI-assisted group through stratified assignment for a 16-week intervention on the learning of vocal music works in Italian, German, and French. Data collection integrated multimodal measurements including cognitive load scales, expert ratings, motion capture, and eye-tracking, with analysis using repeated-measures mixed-factor ANOVA, Bootstrap-based mediation analysis, and thematic analysis. The study found that the XAI scaffolding group's cognitive load reduction reached 38.9%, significantly higher than the control group's 17.0% ( p &lt; 0.001, d = 2.36, 95% CI [1.72, 2.99]), with extraneous cognitive load reduction of 41.2% being the primary contribution; embodied expression total scores improved by 45.0%, with body posture, facial expression, and gesture use dimensions all significantly superior to the control group; language complexity moderated XAI effects, with the advantage most pronounced in German learning ( g = 2.71); the three sequence-disambiguation analyses converged on an independent contribution of language complexity beyond cumulative learning, with the language × group interaction remaining significant after cumulative-exposure adjustment ( <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="M1"> <mml:msubsup> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi>η</mml:mi> </mml:mrow> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi>p</mml:mi> </mml:mrow> <mml:mrow> <mml:mn>2</mml:mn> </mml:mrow> </mml:msubsup> </mml:math> = 0.078, p = 0.007), although complete causal separation awaits future counterbalanced replication; cognitive load played a partial mediating role between XAI scaffolding and embodied expression, with indirect effects accounting for 36.6% of total effects; metacognitive level significantly moderated the mediation pathway; qualitative analysis revealed an “understanding-experiencing-integrating” learning pathway mechanism. This study provides empirical evidence of the potential value of explainable AI in vocal education, offering preliminary theoretical insights and practical guidance for transparent design of intelligent music education systems. These findings warrant replication with larger, multi-site samples and counterbalanced sequencing designs before direct generalization to educational practice.

records.title: Cognition in Mediated Systems: AI Memory, External Thought, Decision Fatigue, and Co-Cognition
records.abstract:
Cognition in Mediated Systems is a five-paper collection examining how memory, reasoning, decision making, and reflection increasingly develop through external tools, digital representations, and artificial intelligence.The collection connects established areas of research including extended cognition, distributed cognition, cognitive artifacts, cognitive offloading, external memory, cognitive load, decision fatigue, collaborative reasoning, Socratic dialogue, and human-AI interaction.The included papers are:Persistent AI Memory and the Extended Architecture of Human Thought
Examines long-context AI, persistent memory, external working memory, personal AI assistants, memory drift, and the emergence of Co-Cognition.Cognitive Artifacts, Representational Tools, and AI-Assisted Thought
Explores how writing, diagrams, notebooks, maps, databases, and AI systems become functional parts of reasoning.Choice Overload, Decision Fatigue, and the Collapse of Useful Constraints
Connects cognitive load and decision fatigue to Constraint Collapse, the weakening of defaults and shared limits that transfers coordination work onto individuals.From Remembering to Retrieving: Cognitive Offloading and Cognitive Drift
Examines how search engines, digital notes, information retrieval, and AI-generated summaries change the architecture of memory and thought.Dialogue as a Distributed Cognitive System
Explains how conversation, reflection, feedback, and human-AI dialogue can produce understanding through a shared cognitive process.Together, the papers describe a broader shift from tools that merely store information to systems that actively participate in what is remembered, organized, interpreted, and carried forward into future reasoning.The collection introduces Co-Cognition as the process through which people and external systems jointly generate, refine, and apply representations. It also examines how these systems can remain coherent and useful while gradually losing context, grounding, or semantic fidelity, creating the conditions for Cognitive Drift, Memory Drift, and Constraint Collapse.

records.title: Cognitive Load and Learned Helplessness: Examining the Psychological Consequences of Instructional Demands
records.venue: Jurnal Theorems (The Original Research of Mathematics)
records.abstract: This study investigates the relationships between the dimensions of cognitive load—namely, intrinsic, extraneous, and germane—and learned helplessness among students. The study is grounded in the premise that students’ learning difficulties may not arise solely from the inherent complexity of learning tasks but also from suboptimal instructional conditions that impose unnecessary cognitive demands, thereby contributing to learned helplessness. A quantitative correlational design was employed involving 150 students as research participants. Data were collected using a 40-item Likert-scale questionnaire ranging from 1 to 4. Instrument validity was established through Pearson product–moment analysis, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.373 to 0.835 (r > 0.160), while reliability indices demonstrated satisfactory internal consistency, as indicated by Cronbach’s alpha coefficients ranging from 0.797 to 0.919. Data normality was confirmed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (p > 0.05). Pearson correlation analysis revealed that extraneous cognitive load exhibited a moderate positive association with learned helplessness (r = 0.543, p < 0.001), suggesting that externally induced cognitive burdens may substantially increase students’ susceptibility to helpless cognitive and behavioral patterns. Intrinsic cognitive load demonstrated a weak positive relationship (r = 0.247, p = 0.002). In contrast, germane cognitive load showed a weak negative association (r = −0.228, p = 0.005), suggesting a potentially protective role in facilitating adaptive learning processes. These findings underscore the critical role of instructional design in regulating learners’ cognitive demands and suggest that reducing unnecessary cognitive burden while fostering meaningful cognitive engagement may be an important strategy for mitigating learned helplessness in educational settings.

records.title: Cognitive Load Reduction in the Context of Artificial Intelligence: A Conceptual Framework for Teachers
records.venue: Asian Journal of Education and Social Studies
records.abstract: Teacher education requires educators to manage multiple pedagogical, administrative, technological, and interpersonal demands that may place substantial pressure on working memory. This conceptual paper examines the relevance of Cognitive Load Theory to teachers and considers how artificial intelligence may support the reduction and management of cognitive load in instructional practice. The study adopts a conceptual research design based on an integrative review and theoretical synthesis of literature concerning cognitive architecture, instructional design, teacher development, and emerging educational technologies. It distinguishes intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load in relation to teachers’ planning, classroom delivery, assessment, feedback, professional collaboration, and reflective practice. On this basis, the paper proposes a provisional AI-supported framework comprising seven interconnected dimensions: goal setting and planning; differentiation and personalisation; real-time classroom delivery; assessment and feedback; emotional and cognitive well-being; collaboration and professional growth; and continuous feedback. The framework positions AI as a support for scheduling, curriculum mapping, lesson co-creation, diagnostics, transcription, grading, reflection, resource recommendation, and adaptive planning. It also emphasises that AI should complement rather than replace professional judgement. Potential risks include over-reliance, reduced critical engagement, privacy concerns, weakened decision-making, and insufficient AI literacy. The proposed framework offers a theoretical basis for examining teacher-focused cognitive offloading, but its feasibility, effectiveness, and ethical implications require empirical validation in diverse educational settings.

records.title: Confounding Components: Problems with Cognitive Load Surveys in Introductory Computer Science
records.venue: Proceedings of the 31st ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education V. 1
records.abstract: Background: Ongoing debates about the structure of cognitive load theory, which traditionally distinguishes among intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load, have important implications for how cognitive load is measured in educational research. Cognitive load theorists debate the distinction between germane and intrinsic load, as well as the reliability of self-reported cognitive load measures and their ability to capture germane load. Prior critiques of cognitive load surveys may equally apply to the widely used measurement tools in computer science education. Purpose: We examine whether validity concerns identified in cognitive load surveys persist in instruments adapted for computer science classrooms. Methods: Fifty-four students in an introductory computer science course were instructed using either live coding or static code examples. Students completed a pre-survey, post-test, and two cognitive load surveys. Internal consistency, predictive validity (association with student performance and instructional mode) and construct alignment between the two surveys were analyzed. Findings: One survey showed high internal consistency for intrinsic and germane cognitive load. Student performance was not predicted by either survey. Additionally, we did not find different instructional modes to correlate with cognitive load. The two surveys were consistent in measuring intrinsic and extraneous load, but inconsistent with respect to germane load. Contributions: Our findings highlight limitations of widely-used cognitive load surveys in computer science education, particularly for germane load, and recommend caution and further validation when using these instruments to assess instructional practices.

records.title: Construct Validation of a Remote Brain Health Assessment Battery to Evaluate Vocational Aptitude and Factors Associated With Cognitive Resilience in the Military: Observational Trial
records.abstract: BACKGROUND: Vocational aptitude and cognitive resilience predict military success, yet current assessments rely on resource-intensive, in-person testing that limits scalability. A brief, self-administered, remotely deployable computerized battery offers a practical solution for large-scale screening and monitoring. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to deploy a set of computerized assessments among National Guard recruits and assess their preliminary construct validity against a standardized aptitude measure and a research-based proxy for cognitive resilience. METHODS: In this observational study, 267 enlisted service members from the Minnesota Army National Guard participated in 2 complementary ethics-approved observational trials: Office of Naval Research Neuropsychometrics and Advancing Research on Mechanisms of Resilience (ARMOR). National Guard soldiers in ARMOR completed the Armed Forces Qualification Test (AFQT), Penn Computerized Neurocognitive Battery (Penn CNB), and a 20-minute computerized brain health assessment battery (BrainHQ) at separate time points over the course of their military careers. BrainHQ assessments consisted of adaptive psychophysical tasks measuring the speed and accuracy of visual and auditory information processing. The battery assessed decision-making speed, emotion-processing speed, selective attention under speeded conditions, working memory capacity for speeded visual elements, verbal memory and learning of speeded speech, and problem-solving speed. The Penn CNB included nonspeeded neuropsychological assessments of executive function, verbal memory, social cognition, and reasoning. Linear regression evaluated the association between BrainHQ performance and AFQT percentiles, and partial correlations assessed associations between conceptually related BrainHQ and Penn CNB subtests. RESULTS: Participants were predominantly young (mean age 19.1 years) and male (178/267, 66.7%). BrainHQ performance was significantly associated with enlistment eligibility and vocational aptitude, as measured by the AFQT (P<.001), after controlling for age and education. The overall model explained 24.4% of the variance in AFQT percentiles (adjusted R2=0.227). The BrainHQ assessment composite was the strongest predictor, uniquely accounting for 19.2% of the variance and supporting the construct validity of aptitude. These associations persisted despite the temporal separation between assessment time points. Quartile analyses showed graded relationships between BrainHQ performance and AFQT eligibility thresholds, with higher BrainHQ performance associated with progressively greater probabilities of meeting higher AFQT benchmarks. Preplanned partial correlations between BrainHQ subtests and standardized neurocognitive measures from the Penn CNB showed significant positive associations (r=0.17-0.25; all P<.001 to .02) with cognitive domains typically associated with cognitive resilience. CONCLUSIONS: A brief, self-administered, and scalable brain health battery demonstrates associations with military vocational aptitude and with neurocognitive domains associated with cognitive resilience. Future studies should evaluate whether integrating these assessments into current practices predicts success in Basic Combat Training, guides military progression, and supports long-term cognitive screening and monitoring across the Armed Forces.

records.title: Correction: School climate and student wellbeing across compulsory education in Portugal: a cross-sectional study of grade-level differences
records.abstract: The school is increasingly challenged not only to meet curricular and academic demands but also to address students' socio-emotional needs. In this context, student well-being and the organizational school climate emerge as key variables in promoting healthy, safe, and motivating learning environments (Cohen et al., 2009;Seligman, 2011). Scientific research has shown that a positive school climate, combined with pedagogical practices that value relationships and student autonomy, significantly contributes to students' holistic development-enhancing not only their academic achievement but also their personal and emotional flourishing (Thapa et al., 2013;Wang & Degol, 2016). In Portugal, research on these topics has gained increasing attention, with studies highlighting the importance of student engagement (Veiga et al., 2014), and the promotion of well-being indicators throughout all stages of schooling (Matos et al., 2015). However, integrated analyses of school climate and student well-being using psychometrically validated instruments applied on a large scale-such as the PERMA-Profiler (Butler & Kern, 2016)-remain scarce. This study addresses this gap by systematically and empirically analysing students' perceptions of school climate and well-being, based on data from a total of 2,842 participants across different educational levels. In addition to exploring developmental trends throughout schooling, the study identifies more vulnerable dimensions-such as school safety and negative emotions-providing useful indicators for the development of more inclusive, protective, and mental health-promoting educational practices. This research contributes to the ongoing discussion by examining students' perceptions of school climate and well-being, with a focus on significant variations observed across the educational trajectory.School climate is an essential construct for understanding school dynamics and their impact on student development. Research has shown that a positive school climate is strongly associated with well-being, academic motivation, and school performance (Cohen et al., 2009;Thapa et al., 2013). The concept of school climate refers to the shared perceptions about the school experience, including norms, values, expectations, interpersonal relationships, pedagogical practices, and the physical conditions of the school environment (National School Climate Council, 2007). This concept is distinct from, yet related to, school culture, with climate being more dynamic and susceptible to short-term changes (Deal & Peterson, 2016). According to Hoy et al. (1991, p. [add page number]), school climate is "...the set of characteristics of the work environment as perceived by the members of the organization, which influences their behaviour and can be described in terms of a set of dimensions that are relatively stable over time." School climate is often conceptualized as a multidimensional construct. According to Cohen et al. (2009), its core dimensions include:(a) physical and emotional safety; (b) quality of interpersonal relationships (respect, support, and empathy); (c) teaching and learning (academic expectations, pedagogical support); and (d) institutional environment (safety, organization, and physical structure). Other authors add elements such as organizational justice (Hoy & Tarter, 2004) and acceptance of diversity (Gottfredson et al., 2005). These dimensions directly affect how students experience the educational context.School Climate Survey Suite (Center on PBIS, 2022) provides a multidimensional profile of climate perceptions. However, it is a self-report instrument and therefore may be influenced by social desirability, response styles, and students' momentary experiences. In addition, some dimensions (e.g., safety and discipline) may be particularly sensitive to contextual events and may show different meanings across age/grade groups. These limitations are relevant when interpreting developmental trends across compulsory education and underscore the importance of examining dimension-level reliability and model fit in the target population. Programs such as Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS) and Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) interventions have demonstrated effectiveness in improving school climate and student well-being (Durlak et al., 2011). These approaches promote healthy interpersonal relationships, empathy, emotional regulation, and safe learning environments. Benbenishty and Astor (2005) emphasize the importance of involving the entire school community-students, teachers, school leadership, and families-in building positive school climates centred on inclusion, mutual respect, and emotional safety. School climate is a key factor in promoting student well-being and educational success. The scientific literature acknowledges its multidimensional nature and its strong relationship with psychological, pedagogical, and institutional factors. Studies on school climate conducted in Portugal provide a solid foundation for understanding the impact of organizational climate and student well-being.Student well-being is considered a fundamental pillar for academic success and the holistic development of children and adolescents. Research in education and psychology has increasingly emphasized the importance of school environments that not only foster academic achievement but also support students ' mental, emotional, and social health (O'Connor et al., 2011;Pollard & Lee, 2003;). Well-being is a multidimensional and complex concept, encompassing both subjective aspects (e.g., happiness and life satisfaction) and objective aspects (e.g., living conditions, health, and social relationships). In the school context, student well-being can be understood as a sense of physical, emotional, and psychological wellbeing, in conjunction with students' ability to cope with the daily challenges of school life (OECD, 2017). Seligman (2011) proposed one of the most influential models in positive psychology: the PERMA model, which defines well-being based on five core dimensions: P -Positive emotions; E -Engagement; R -Positive relationships; M -Meaning; A -Accomplishment. Building on this model, authors such as Butler and Kern (2016) have added complementary dimensions such as physical health, vitality, and negative emotions, offering a broader perspective on overall well-being. More recent research shows that learning environments that promote autonomy and supportive relationships are predictive of higher levels of well-being, particularly in the dimensions of the PERMA model (Cobo-Rendón et al., 2024). On the other hand, Lindskov (2025) advocates for a conceptualization of wellbeing that focuses more explicitly on students' voices, recognizing them as key agents in defining their own flourishing. These recent contributions expand the relevance of analysing perceptions of well-being across different stages of compulsory education.Authors such as Csikszentmihalyi (2002) and Fredrickson (2001) have highlighted the role of positive emotions and personal strengths in promoting well-being. The application of these principles to the educational context gave rise to the concept of positive education, which integrates teaching with the promotion of psychological well-being (Seligman et al., 2009;Waters, 2011). Deci and Ryan (1985) developed Self-Determination Theory, which posits that well-being depends on the fulfilment of three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness. When these needs are met within the school context, students demonstrate greater intrinsic motivation, better emotional adjustment, and higher satisfaction with school (Jang et al., 2010;Niemiec & Ryan, 2009;). Bronfenbrenner (1979) offers a systemic perspective on human development, in which well-being is influenced by multiple levels of interaction-from the individual to interpersonal relationships, and the school, community, and broader social environments. The school is seen as one of the primary microsystems that can either support or undermine students' well-being, depending on the quality of its practices, relationships, and physical environment.The assessment of well-being should reflect its multidimensional nature. The PERMA-Profiler (Butler & Kern, 2016) is one of the most widely used scales to assess the five dimensions of well-being proposed by Seligman, supplemented by items on negative emotions, physical health, and vitality. Research suggests that this scale demonstrates good internal consistency, factorial validity, and cultural sensitivity (Kern et al., 2015). Other instruments include the KIDSCREEN (Ravens-Sieberer et al., 2005), which focuses on the health and quality of life of children and adolescents, and the Student Subjective Wellbeing Questionnaire (Renshaw et al., 2015), which emphasizes emotional and motivational aspects of school well-being. The PERMA-Profiler offers a broad operationalization of flourishing, but it also relies on self-report and single-informant data, which may not fully capture context-specific school experiences or students' implicit/behavioural functioning. Moreover, some facets (e.g., engagement/flow-like experiences) can be challenging for younger students to evaluate with precision, which may affect comparability across grade levels. For these reasons, interpreting differences across educational stages benefits from reporting dimensionlevel reliability and acknowledging potential developmental/measurement non-equivalence.Promoting well-being in school settings requires an integrated and systemic approach.Programs such as Positive Education, the Mindfulness in Schools Project (Weare, 2014), and Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) have shown positive effects on students' mental health, interpersonal relationships, and behaviour (Durlak et al., 2011). Waters and Loton (2019) advocate for a positive education-based approach that combines the teaching of social and emotional skills with pedagogical practices that foster optimism, gratitude, resilience, and a sense of purpose. Student well-being is a key indicator of educational quality and a central goal of inclusive and humanistic schools. Understanding the factors that influence it, as well as its manifestations across the school years, enables schools to design more effective policies and practices focused on fostering healthy learning environments. The PERMA model provides a solid foundation for such analysis and for the development of interventions aligned with students' holistic growth.The school climate is an essential construct for understanding school dynamics and their impact on student development. Research has consistently shown that a positive school climate is strongly associated with well-being, academic motivation, and school performance (Cohen et al., 2009;Thapa et al., 2013;Wang & Degol, 2016). More recent studies confirm that positive school climates not only support students' socio-emotional adjustment but are also linked to better academic outcomes and lower dropout risk (Podiya et al., 2025).Furthermore, the bibliometric analysis by Bentsalo et al. (2025) identified safety, inclusion, and the quality of interpersonal relationships as central pillars of student well-being.In schools described as having a positive climate, there is greater student engagement, lower incidence of emotional and behavioural problems, and better mental health (Suldo et al., 2022;Wang & Degol, 2016). Seligman's PERMA model (2011), which structures well-being around five pillars-Positive Emotions, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment-can be effectively integrated with school climate theory. Kern, Waters, Adler, and White (2015) demonstrated that schools promoting healthy relationships and a sense of purpose support students' psychological flourishing. However, students' perceptions of school climate tend to deteriorate as they advance through school years (Way et al., 2007).Studies show that secondary school students report lower school connectedness, reduced teacher support, and increased feelings of insecurity (Eccles & Roeser, 2011). This trend highlights the importance of tailored interventions across different stages of education.Relationships with peers, teachers, and families have consistently been identified as key predictors of student well-being (Danielsen et al., 2009). Supportive and positive relationships foster a sense of belonging and safety, whereas experiences of rejection or bullying have profoundly negative effects (Suldo et al., 2012). School climate, understood as the quality of the relational, physical, and pedagogical environment, directly influences student well-being (Thapa et al., 2013). Positive school climates promote higher levels of engagement, self-esteem, and mental health. In contrast, excessive academic workload, performance-centered assessment, and peer competition are factors that contribute to academic stress and anxiety (Putwain, 2007). On the other hand, pedagogical strategies that value the learning process, autonomy, and constructive feedback tend to foster greater wellbeing (Martin & Marsh, 2006). Longitudinal studies have shown that student well-being tends to decline throughout compulsory education, especially during the transition to secondary school (Eccles & Roeser, 2011;Gilman & Huebner, 2006).
